unit.name: Cultural Transmission & Research Methods
unit.subtitle: Key sociological concepts, the four perspectives, and the research methods used to investigate the social world.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat crime and deviance as synonymous. The spec defines them as overlapping but distinct: crime breaks the law; deviance violates social norms (which may or may not be illegal). Some acts are deviant but not criminal (queue-jumping, talking loudly in a library); some are criminal but not seen as widely deviant (minor speeding). Spec section 6.1 explicitly requires students to explain 'social construction of crime and deviance'.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 6.1 — 'social construction of concepts of crime and deviance'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Sociological perspectives confused with each other
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students collapse functionalism and consensus, and Marxism and any conflict view. Each has a precise position: functionalism = society as an integrated whole, institutions perform necessary functions; Marxism = society as class conflict between bourgeoisie and proletariat; feminism = society as patriarchal; interactionism = micro-level meanings, labels and interactions. The spec lists these four and requires students to compare and contrast them on every topic.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, recurring framing 'conflict versus consensus debate' across sections 2.4, 3.1, 5.1, 6.4.

common_misconceptions.topic: Common-sense answers instead of sociological terminology
common_misconceptions.misconception: Examiner reports flag this as the single biggest discriminator between bands. Students write 'rich people don't get caught' instead of 'differential enforcement of the law'; 'girls behave better' instead of 'patriarchal control of women'. Generic synonyms cap an answer below the sociological-terminology mark band even if the substance is correct.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024 (eduqas.co.uk/media/ocvnygux/eduqas-gcse-sociology-final-report-s24-e.pdf) — 'Less successful answers were more commonsense in style and lacked the accurate use of terminology'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Hidden curriculum confused with the formal curriculum
common_misconceptions.misconception: The 2024 Component 1 question 5c on the hidden curriculum was a low-scoring item. Students described what schools teach (subjects on the timetable) instead of the unwritten lessons of obedience, hierarchy, punctuality and gender norms transmitted alongside academic content. The spec names hidden curriculum in 3.2 — students must define it as the implicit, informal lessons, link to Bowles and Gintis correspondence theory, and give concrete examples.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024 (eduqas.co.uk/media/ocvnygux/eduqas-gcse-sociology-final-report-s24-e.pdf) — Component 1 question 5c challenge flagged.

common_misconceptions.topic: Studies attributed to the wrong sociologist
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse the named pairings: Parsons = primary socialisation; Oakley = conventional family; Willmott and Young = symmetrical family; Bowles and Gintis = correspondence principle; Willis = counter school cultures; Becker = labelling; Merton = anomie; Heidensohn = female conformity; Cohen = delinquent subcultures; Carlen = women, crime and poverty; Davis and Moore = functionalist stratification; Townsend = relative deprivation; Murray = underclass; Walby = patriarchy; Chambliss = differential law enforcement; Hargreaves = labelling in classrooms; Becky Francis = patriarchal schools; Devine = affluent worker; Rapoports = five types of diversity; Zaretsky = Marxist family; Delphy and Leonard = patriarchal family.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification — named theorist pairings throughout sections 2-6.

common_misconceptions.topic: Functionalists confused with conservatives on power and inequality
common_misconceptions.misconception: The 2024 examiner report noted: 'Stronger candidates were able to identify that Functionalists accept that there are power differences in society, but that these are inevitable and necessary.' Weaker students assume functionalists deny inequality exists. The Davis and Moore position is that stratification is FUNCTIONAL — necessary, not invisible.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024 (eduqas.co.uk/media/ocvnygux/eduqas-gcse-sociology-final-report-s24-e.pdf) — explicit comment on the functionalist position on power.

common_misconceptions.topic: Official statistics treated as objective truth
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students cite police-recorded crime figures or divorce statistics as definitive. The spec is explicit: official statistics have strengths AND weaknesses (4.1, 6.5). The dark figure of crime (6.5) is the spec's worked example of why official statistics under-represent crime. Always evaluate, don't just cite.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, sections 4.1 (sources of secondary data) and 6.5 (dark figure of crime, usefulness of data).

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'poverty' as one concept. The spec needs the distinction — absolute (lacking resources for basic survival) vs relative (lacking what is normal in a given society). Townsend's relative deprivation (5.5) includes social participation, not just material need.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 5.5 — 'absolute and relative poverty, including the work of Townsend on relative deprivation'.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mis-allocate examples to Weber's three types: traditional = legitimacy from custom (monarchy); charismatic = legitimacy from personal qualities (a magnetic political leader); rational-legal = legitimacy from formal rules and offices (an elected MP, a judge). Students often call any leader 'charismatic' and mis-tag elected officials as 'traditional'.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 5.2 — 'Weberian theory of authority: traditional, charismatic and rational-legal'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Medical and social models of disability collapsed into one
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe disability as a single concept. The spec (5.3) demands the binary: medical model = disability is the impairment in the individual; social model = disability is created by societal barriers. Students must give one example of each (e.g. medical model: a wheelchair user is 'disabled' by their inability to walk; social model: a wheelchair user is 'disabled' by the absence of ramps).
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 5.3 — 'with specific reference to disability: medical and social models of disability'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Methods evaluation reduced to a generic list
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students recite generic strengths and weaknesses of methods without applying them to a specific research context. The spec explicitly demands evaluation IN CONTEXT. A 12-mark methods Evaluate question expects 'why participant observation is risky for studying gangs specifically', not 'observation is time-consuming' in general.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 4.2 — 'value, practical application and strengths and weaknesses of different methods'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Ethical issues treated as a checklist
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students list 'consent, confidentiality, harm' as boxes to tick rather than reasoning about which apply in a given study and how researchers address them. The spec explicitly requires 'strategies used by sociologists to address issues' (4.5) — students must propose practical solutions (anonymisation, debriefing, withdrawal rights), not just name the principle.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification, section 4.5 — 'strategies used by sociologists to address issues'.

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice: Students leave items blank or guess without reading all four options. With 100 marks per paper, a single multiple choice mark is non-trivial. Read every distractor — plausible-sounding wrong answers are deliberately included to catch confusion of named sociologists or perspectives.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Define: Students give an example instead of a definition. A 'Define' question expects a meaning expressed in sociological language — 'patriarchy' is 'a system in which men hold power and women are disadvantaged', not 'when men are in charge of the family'. Each mark usually = one element of the definition.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Identify and Describe: Students identify a feature but fail to describe it. The structure expected is identify (1 mark) plus a developed description (2 marks). Two short sentences score lower than one developed point with sociological vocabulary.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Describe: Students describe one feature when 4 marks usually requires either two developed points or four discrete features. Linking to a named sociologist or concept lifts the answer into the higher mark band.
student_errors_by_question_type.9 marks — Discuss: Students give a one-sided answer or list points without judgement. 2024 examiner report is explicit: 'A common theme on these 9-mark questions is the need to evaluate and analyse.' Top answers present at least two perspectives by name and reach a supported conclusion.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Evaluate: Students recite knowledge without judgement. The 12-mark Evaluate is the most heavily AO3-weighted question. Top-band answers compare and contrast at least two named perspectives, cite at least two named sociologists, weigh evidence on each side, and arrive at a reasoned conclusion. AO3 is 20% of the qualification — students who skip evaluation cap below grade 7.

topic_weighting_notes: Two papers, 100 marks each, 50% of GCSE each. Component 1 = Cultural Transmission + Families + Education + Research Methods. Component 2 = Stratification + Crime & Deviance + Applied Methods of Sociological Enquiry. Equal weighting forces equal revision time. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 2.)

AO weighting is AO1 40%, AO2 40%, AO3 20% — same per component. Students often overweight AO1 (recall) at the expense of AO2 (application) and AO3 (evaluation). The 9-mark and 12-mark extended response questions are where AO3 is awarded — extended-response practice is non-negotiable. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 3.1.)

A minimum of 15% of the available marks in each examination series is awarded for knowledge and understanding in relation to Research Methods. This is a STANDING REQUIREMENT — research methods will appear on every paper, every year. Drill methods in topic context (methods on family research, methods on crime research). (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 3.1.)

Component 2 contains a separate 'Applied Methods of Sociological Enquiry' strand (topic 7) that overlaps with research methods (topic 4) but is assessed differently — the applied strand demands students DESIGN a study and INTERPRET data, not just describe methods. Allocate revision time to scenario-led applied-methods practice, distinct from method-by-method drilling. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 2.2.)

Spec content is set in a UK context except where otherwise stated. UK-relevant examples (Crime Survey for England and Wales, ONS divorce statistics, UK education policy) are expected. Global examples are appropriate where the spec invites them — family forms (2.1, including 'one-child family policy in China', polygamy, arranged marriage) and 'impact of globalisation' on poverty (5.5). (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 2 'study the content in a UK context except where otherwise stated'.)

Welsh-context note for WJEC variant: while the specifications are byte-identical, WJEC students sit in Wales. UK-wide examples remain valid for both. Where examples are genuinely English-only (English/Welsh divorce reform 2022 timing, Welsh policy on academies/free schools differing from England's), note jurisdictional scope explicitly without making it a board-specific statement. Lessons stay neutrally phrased.
current_spec_changes: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology has been taught from September 2017, first awarded 2019, and has been in steady state since. Current published version is Version 2 January 2019. No spec content changes are scheduled for 2026 exams. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification cover page.)

Examination timetable for Summer 2026 is published by WJEC; the qualification is linear (all assessment at the end of the course, in the same series). (Source: WJEC and Eduqas Summer 2026 examination timetable, wjec.co.uk/media/ovdbnkhj/summer-2026-wales-and-eduqas-gcse-october-2025.pdf.)
The qualification is linear and contains no controlled assessment or coursework component. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 4.)

The 2024 examiner report flagged Component 1 question 5c (hidden curriculum) as the lowest-scoring item, with most candidates struggling to define hidden curriculum precisely. Future builds should foreground this concept in the education unit. (Source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024.)
pedagogical_notes: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — disciplinary literacy is critical. Sociology has dense specialist vocabulary. Teach a focused 6-8 term glossary at the start of every lesson and require precise use in extended responses. The 2024 examiner report explicitly flagged that 'less successful answers were more commonsense in style and lacked the accurate use of terminology' — generic synonyms cost marks. (Source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report; Eduqas Examiners' Report Summer 2024.)

EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (effect size +8 months) — explicitly model how to structure a 9-mark Discuss or 12-mark Evaluate response: argument for (cite a perspective and a named study), argument against (cite a contrasting perspective and study), supported judgement. Students do not do this automatically. Use shared-write worked examples before independent practice. (Source: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning Guidance Report.)

Retrieval practice — the named sociologists and their key ideas form a finite list of about 20 pairings. Short, frequent low-stakes retrieval quizzes (study + concept + perspective) outperform single long revision sessions. Each lesson ends with a 5-question knowledge check for this reason. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit.)

Compare-and-contrast as a teaching frame — every spec topic asks students to compare perspectives. Build every lesson around a 4-column perspective grid (functionalist / Marxist / feminist / interactionist or New Right where relevant). Students who internalise the grid have an instant scaffold for any 12-mark Evaluate question. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification — recurring 'conflict versus consensus debate' framing across topics.)

Dual coding — pair every named sociologist with a labelled visual (Bowles and Gintis = school-to-workplace flow diagram showing the correspondence principle; Walby = the six structures of patriarchy as a hexagon). Pair the visual with a one-sentence verbal summary. Ask students to reproduce both halves from memory. (Source: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit.)

Sensitive topic handling — sociology covers contested issues (gender roles, ethnic inequality, family diversity, crime, religion, sexuality, disability). Present each as legitimate disagreement between named perspectives rather than as a single authorial line. Treat New Right, Marxist and feminist views with equal descriptive seriousness. This protects the impartiality required by the spec's debate-and-evaluate brief and supports DfE political-impartiality framework. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification section 1.1 'critically analyse information and use evidence to make informed arguments'; DfE Political impartiality in schools guidance 2022.)

Application as comprehension — many extended response questions are stem-led, presenting an extract or item that students must respond to. Train students to read the stem TWICE: once for content, once for the perspective hooks the examiner has signalled. Every paragraph in the response should reference the stem at least once. (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification — 'reading and responding to extracts which illustrate the different views of sociologists'.)

Data interpretation as a discrete skill — Eduqas/WJEC topic 7.2 explicitly demands students interpret graphs, charts and tables. This is a unique requirement vs other boards. Practise reading data BEFORE moving to causes — present one set of attainment-gap data without explanation, get students to describe the pattern, only then explain. Mirrors the spec separation of patterns (3.3, 6.3) from factors (3.4-3.5, 6.4). (Source: Eduqas/WJEC GCSE Sociology specification sections 7.1, 7.2.)

Examiner-flagged concept: hidden curriculum. 2024 Component 1 5c was the lowest-scoring item — students confused hidden with formal curriculum. Future cohorts must drill the definition (unwritten, implicit lessons of conformity, hierarchy, punctuality, gender norms) and the named link to Bowles and Gintis correspondence theory. (Source: Eduqas GCSE Sociology Examiners' Report Summer 2024.)

_source_meta.source_lesson_title: What Is Sociology? The Sociological Approach

source.content_html:
What Is Sociology?

Sociology is the disciplined study of how society works. Rather than explaining human behaviour through individual personality or biology, sociologists look at the social forces that shape people’s lives — the groups they belong to, the rules they follow, and the inequalities built into the world around them. Sociology asks questions such as: why do some groups consistently achieve less in education? Why are some people more likely to be labelled criminal? What holds society together, and what tears it apart?

Crucially, sociology is not common sense. Common sense might say that poverty is caused by laziness. Sociology investigates the social structures that distribute wealth unequally, the institutions that reproduce disadvantage, and the processes by which labels are attached to whole groups of people. The discipline demands evidence, theory and critical thinking.

Key Fact

The core concepts of sociology are society, socialisation, norms, values, roles, culture, power and authority. These eight concepts appear across every topic in your exam and underpin every sociological argument you will make.

Socialisation: How Society Gets Into People

Socialisation is the mechanism through which society reproduces itself in the next generation. Through socialisation, individuals learn what behaviours are expected of them, what counts as right and wrong, and how to perform the social roles assigned to them. Without socialisation, the shared understandings that allow society to function would collapse.

Primary socialisation happens in the family, in early childhood. It is here that children first learn language, basic rules of behaviour, emotional responses and a sense of who they are. Parsons, writing from a functionalist perspective, argued that the family is the irreplaceable site of primary socialisation because it transmits the core values of society to each new generation.

Secondary socialisation occurs through agencies outside the family — schools, peer groups, workplaces and the mass media. Each of these agencies reinforces (or sometimes challenges) the values first taught in the home. Feminists such as Oakley have highlighted that secondary socialisation through toys, media and peer groups reinforces gendered expectations from a very young age.

Norms, Values, Roles and Culture

Norms are the unwritten rules of behaviour that tell people how to act in specific situations — how to greet a stranger, how to behave in a classroom, what to wear at a funeral. Unlike formal laws, norms are enforced informally through social approval or disapproval. Values are the deeper moral beliefs that lie beneath norms — for example, the norm of queuing in shops reflects an underlying value of fairness.

A role is a set of expected behaviours attached to a social position. The teacher role, the parent role, the police officer role — each comes with a bundle of norms about how the person in that position should act. These roles exist independently of the individuals who fill them; a new teacher steps into a role that was there before them and will remain after they leave. Together, norms, values and roles make up culture — the entire shared way of life of a society.

Power is the ability to get others to act in ways they might not otherwise choose. It can be exercised through force, persuasion or the control of resources. Authority is the legitimate exercise of power — power that others accept as rightful. Weber identified three types of authority: traditional (legitimacy from custom and inheritance, e.g. the monarchy), charismatic (legitimacy from a leader’s personal qualities), and rational-legal (legitimacy from formal rules and elected offices, e.g. a judge or elected MP).

Different perspectives disagree on who holds power and why. Functionalists argue power is distributed through legitimate authority for the benefit of society as a whole. Marxists argue power is concentrated in the hands of the bourgeoisie (the capitalist class), who use it to maintain their dominance over the proletariat. Feminists argue that patriarchal structures give men disproportionate power over women in both public and private life. Interactionists are more interested in how power operates in micro-level face-to-face interactions — for instance, how labels imposed by powerful actors (teachers, police, doctors) can define and constrain less powerful individuals.

Consensus Versus Conflict: The Central Debate

One of the most important debates in sociology is between consensus and conflict perspectives on what holds society together. This debate runs through every topic you will study.

Consensus perspectives — most notably functionalism — argue that society is held together by shared norms and values. Most people, most of the time, agree on the basic rules of social life. Institutions such as the family, education and religion serve positive functions by transmitting these shared values and maintaining social order. From this view, inequality, where it exists, reflects the different functional importance of different roles, not exploitation.

Conflict perspectives — most notably Marxism and feminism — argue that society is characterised by fundamental divisions and inequalities. For Marxists, the key division is class: the bourgeoisie own the means of production and exploit the labour of the proletariat. For feminists, the key division is gender: patriarchal structures systematically disadvantage women. Both argue that the apparent consensus in society is not genuine agreement but the product of false consciousness or ideological control.

A frequent error is to treat sociological knowledge as “just common sense.” Sociology challenges common sense systematically. Common sense explanations are often ethnocentric (culture-bound), unreflective about their own assumptions, and unsupported by evidence. Sociology builds theories from evidence, tests them against data, and acknowledges that its own knowledge is socially produced and therefore open to critical scrutiny. The discipline asks: whose common sense? Common sense in 1950s Britain treated racial segregation as natural; sociology helped expose the social construction of race and the institutional processes that produced racial inequality.

Key Fact

Consensus perspectives (e.g. functionalism) argue society is held together by shared norms and values. Conflict perspectives (e.g. Marxism, feminism) argue society is divided by class, gender or other inequalities and that apparent harmony conceals exploitation or oppression.
source.exam_tip_html: On a 2-mark Define question, give a definition — not an example. Students often write “norms are like saying please and thank you” when they should write “norms are unwritten rules that govern expected behaviour in social situations.” Each mark usually rewards one element of the definition, so a complete sociological definition earns both marks. On a 12-mark Discuss, always state which perspective you are describing before you describe it. Writing “Some people think…” earns no marks. Writing “From a functionalist perspective, Parsons argued that…” immediately signals to the examiner that you understand the perspectives framework and are operating at the higher mark bands.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sociology studies society through key concepts — socialisation, norms, values, roles, culture, power and authority — rather than reducing behaviour to individual biology or personality.
  • Primary socialisation (family) and secondary socialisation (school, peer groups, media) are the two main processes by which individuals learn the norms and values of their society.
  • The consensus vs conflict debate is fundamental: functionalists argue society is held together by shared values; Marxists and feminists argue it is divided by class or gender inequalities concealed by false consciousness or patriarchal ideology.

source.content_html:
What Is Sociology?

Sociology is the disciplined study of how society works. Rather than explaining human behaviour through individual personality or biology, sociologists look at the social forces that shape people’s lives — the groups they belong to, the rules they follow, and the inequalities built into the world around them. Sociology asks questions such as: why do some groups consistently achieve less in education? Why are some people more likely to be labelled criminal? What holds society together, and what tears it apart?

Crucially, sociology is not common sense. Common sense might say that poverty is caused by laziness. Sociology investigates the social structures that distribute wealth unequally, the institutions that reproduce disadvantage, and the processes by which labels are attached to whole groups of people. The discipline demands evidence, theory and critical thinking.

Key Fact

The core concepts of sociology are society, socialisation, norms, values, roles, culture, power and authority. These eight concepts appear across every topic in your exam and underpin every sociological argument you will make.

Socialisation: How Society Gets Into People

Socialisation is the mechanism through which society reproduces itself in the next generation. Through socialisation, individuals learn what behaviours are expected of them, what counts as right and wrong, and how to perform the social roles assigned to them. Without socialisation, the shared understandings that allow society to function would collapse.

Primary socialisation happens in the family, in early childhood. It is here that children first learn language, basic rules of behaviour, emotional responses and a sense of who they are. Parsons, writing from a functionalist perspective, argued that the family is the irreplaceable site of primary socialisation because it transmits the core values of society to each new generation.

Secondary socialisation occurs through agencies outside the family — schools, peer groups, workplaces and the mass media. Each of these agencies reinforces (or sometimes challenges) the values first taught in the home. Feminists such as Oakley have highlighted that secondary socialisation through toys, media and peer groups reinforces gendered expectations from a very young age.

Norms, Values, Roles and Culture

Norms are the unwritten rules of behaviour that tell people how to act in specific situations — how to greet a stranger, how to behave in a classroom, what to wear at a funeral. Unlike formal laws, norms are enforced informally through social approval or disapproval. Values are the deeper moral beliefs that lie beneath norms — for example, the norm of queuing in shops reflects an underlying value of fairness.

A role is a set of expected behaviours attached to a social position. The teacher role, the parent role, the police officer role — each comes with a bundle of norms about how the person in that position should act. These roles exist independently of the individuals who fill them; a new teacher steps into a role that was there before them and will remain after they leave. Together, norms, values and roles make up culture — the entire shared way of life of a society.

Power is the ability to get others to act in ways they might not otherwise choose. It can be exercised through force, persuasion or the control of resources. Authority is the legitimate exercise of power — power that others accept as rightful. Weber identified three types of authority: traditional (legitimacy from custom and inheritance, e.g. the monarchy), charismatic (legitimacy from a leader’s personal qualities), and rational-legal (legitimacy from formal rules and elected offices, e.g. a judge or elected MP).

Different perspectives disagree on who holds power and why. Functionalists argue power is distributed through legitimate authority for the benefit of society as a whole. Marxists argue power is concentrated in the hands of the bourgeoisie (the capitalist class), who use it to maintain their dominance over the proletariat. Feminists argue that patriarchal structures give men disproportionate power over women in both public and private life. Interactionists are more interested in how power operates in micro-level face-to-face interactions — for instance, how labels imposed by powerful actors (teachers, police, doctors) can define and constrain less powerful individuals.

Consensus Versus Conflict: The Central Debate

One of the most important debates in sociology is between consensus and conflict perspectives on what holds society together. This debate runs through every topic you will study.

Consensus perspectives — most notably functionalism — argue that society is held together by shared norms and values. Most people, most of the time, agree on the basic rules of social life. Institutions such as the family, education and religion serve positive functions by transmitting these shared values and maintaining social order. From this view, inequality, where it exists, reflects the different functional importance of different roles, not exploitation.

Conflict perspectives — most notably Marxism and feminism — argue that society is characterised by fundamental divisions and inequalities. For Marxists, the key division is class: the bourgeoisie own the means of production and exploit the labour of the proletariat. For feminists, the key division is gender: patriarchal structures systematically disadvantage women. Both argue that the apparent consensus in society is not genuine agreement but the product of false consciousness or ideological control.

A frequent error is to treat sociological knowledge as “just common sense.” Sociology challenges common sense systematically. Common sense explanations are often ethnocentric (culture-bound), unreflective about their own assumptions, and unsupported by evidence. Sociology builds theories from evidence, tests them against data, and acknowledges that its own knowledge is socially produced and therefore open to critical scrutiny. The discipline asks: whose common sense? Common sense in 1950s Britain treated racial segregation as natural; sociology helped expose the social construction of race and the institutional processes that produced racial inequality.

Key Fact

Consensus perspectives (e.g. functionalism) argue society is held together by shared norms and values. Conflict perspectives (e.g. Marxism, feminism) argue society is divided by class, gender or other inequalities and that apparent harmony conceals exploitation or oppression.
source.exam_tip_html: On a 2-mark Define question, give a definition — not an example. Students often write “norms are like saying please and thank you” when they should write “norms are unwritten rules that govern expected behaviour in social situations.” Each mark usually rewards one element of the definition, so a complete sociological definition earns both marks. On a 12-mark Discuss, always state which perspective you are describing before you describe it. Writing “Some people think…” earns no marks. Writing “From a functionalist perspective, Parsons argued that…” immediately signals to the examiner that you understand the perspectives framework and are operating at the higher mark bands.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sociology studies society through key concepts — socialisation, norms, values, roles, culture, power and authority — rather than reducing behaviour to individual biology or personality.
  • Primary socialisation (family) and secondary socialisation (school, peer groups, media) are the two main processes by which individuals learn the norms and values of their society.
  • The consensus vs conflict debate is fundamental: functionalists argue society is held together by shared values; Marxists and feminists argue it is divided by class or gender inequalities concealed by false consciousness or patriarchal ideology.

source.content_html:
Why Perspectives Matter

A sociological perspective is a theoretical lens through which sociologists interpret the social world. No single perspective commands universal agreement; instead, sociology is a discipline of competing theoretical frameworks, each illuminating different aspects of society. The AQA specification names four perspectives that you must know, compare and apply to every topic: functionalism, Marxism, feminism and interactionism.

A key skill in sociology is being able to describe what each perspective argues, who the named sociologists are, and how each perspective differs from the others. In your extended responses, stating the perspective before making a claim is essential: “From a Marxist perspective…” or “Feminists argue that…” signals to the examiner that you are operating at the level of sociological analysis rather than personal opinion.

Functionalism: Society as a Working System

Functionalism is a consensus perspective. Functionalists argue that society resembles a biological organism: each institution (the family, education, religion, the economy) performs necessary functions that contribute to the survival and stability of the whole. Society is held together by value consensus — a broad shared agreement on core values that enables cooperation and social order.

Durkheim is the founding functionalist thinker. Parsons extended this framework to argue that the family performs two irreplaceable functions: the primary socialisation of children and the stabilisation of adult personalities. For functionalists, social inequality, where it exists, can serve a functional purpose: Davis and Moore later argued that higher rewards for more demanding roles act as incentives for talented individuals to train for them, ensuring that important positions are filled effectively.

Critics argue that functionalism is politically conservative: it tends to justify existing arrangements as functional and necessary, making it difficult to explain persistent inequality as anything other than a natural sorting mechanism. Marxists and feminists argue that functionalism ignores the role of power and conflict in shaping institutions that ostensibly serve “society” but in practice serve dominant groups.

Key Fact

Functionalism is a consensus perspective: it sees shared norms and values as the foundation of social order. Marxism, feminism and conflict perspectives argue instead that society is shaped by power and inequality that serves dominant groups.

Marxism: Society as Class Conflict

Marxism is a conflict perspective. Marxists argue that capitalist society is fundamentally divided between the bourgeoisie (who own the means of production) and the proletariat (who must sell their labour). All major social institutions — the family, education, the law, religion — serve to reproduce and legitimate this exploitative relationship. The ruling class maintains control not only through economic power but through ideological control: promoting ideas (via the media, religion, education) that make the existing order appear natural and just.

Marx argued that the dominant ideas of any age are the ideas of the dominant class. Workers are kept in a state of false consciousness, accepting their own subordination as inevitable. Bowles and Gintis later applied this framework to education, arguing that schools reproduce the workforce capitalism needs through the correspondence principle — matching attitudes and behaviours in school (obedience, punctuality, deference to authority) to those required in the workplace.

Functionalism: Society is based on consensus; institutions perform functions for the benefit of society as a whole; inequality reflects functional necessity. Key thinkers: Durkheim, Parsons, Davis and Moore.

Marxism: Society is based on class conflict; institutions serve the interests of the ruling class; inequality is the product of exploitation, not merit. Key thinkers: Marx, Bowles and Gintis, Zaretsky.

Both are macro (or structural) perspectives: they explain individual behaviour by reference to large-scale social structures. They differ on whether those structures are consensual or coercive.

Feminism: Society as Patriarchal

Feminism is a conflict perspective that focuses on gender inequality. Feminists argue that society is patriarchal — structured so that men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged. Walby identified six structures of patriarchy: paid employment, household production, culture, sexuality, violence and the state. Together these operate across public and private life to maintain male dominance.

Feminism is not a single perspective but a family of related arguments. Liberal feminism argues that legal reforms and changing attitudes can achieve gender equality. Marxist feminism (e.g. Zaretsky) argues that women’s oppression is tied to capitalism: women provide unpaid domestic labour that sustains the workforce, benefiting the capitalist class. Radical feminism argues that patriarchy is an autonomous system of male domination that cannot be dismantled simply by legal or economic reform; it requires a fundamental reorganisation of social relations between men and women.

Key Fact

Feminism, Marxism and functionalism are all macro perspectives: they explain social behaviour through large-scale structures (patriarchy, class, value consensus). Interactionism is a micro perspective: it focuses on face-to-face interactions and the meanings individuals construct in everyday life.

Interactionism: Society as Meaning-Making

Interactionism focuses on the small-scale, everyday interactions through which individuals construct and negotiate meaning. Rather than starting with large-scale structures, interactionists ask: what does this situation mean to the people in it? How do labels applied by powerful actors shape individuals’ self-concepts and behaviour?

Becker’s labelling theory (Outsiders, 1963) is the key interactionist contribution to crime and deviance. Becker argued that deviance is not an inherent quality of an act but a label applied by those with the power to define and enforce rules. A master status — such as “criminal” or “truant” — can come to override all other aspects of a person’s identity, shaping how others see them and how they see themselves. If a student is labelled as a troublemaker, teachers may interpret all their behaviour through that lens, and the student may eventually internalise the label (the self-fulfilling prophecy).

Students often conflate interactionism with the other three perspectives. A clear distinction: functionalism, Marxism and feminism are all structural (macro) perspectives — they explain individual behaviour by reference to large-scale forces (value consensus, class, patriarchy). Interactionism is a micro perspective — it starts from the individual interaction and the meanings people construct. Both levels of analysis are valid and complementary: structural perspectives explain patterns (why working-class students underachieve on average); interactionist perspectives explain processes (how specific labels applied by specific teachers contribute to that pattern in practice).
source.exam_tip_html: The 12-mark Discuss question will often invite you to compare perspectives. The most common error is to describe all four perspectives without evaluating them — which caps you in the Developing tier. To reach Secure or Mastering, you must: compare (e.g. “Unlike functionalists, who argue…, Marxists contend…”), evaluate (e.g. “A limitation of the functionalist view is that it ignores…”), and judge (e.g. “On balance, the feminist perspective is more convincing because…”). Never describe all four perspectives as equally valid without explaining why you find one more or less convincing than another. The examiner is looking for a reasoned judgement, not a balanced description.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Functionalism (consensus, macro) argues society is held together by shared values and institutions perform necessary functions. Marxism (conflict, macro) argues society is divided by class exploitation and institutions serve the ruling class.
  • Feminism (conflict, macro) argues society is patriarchal — structured to maintain male power. Three strands: liberal (legal reform), Marxist (capitalism + gender oppression), radical (patriarchy as autonomous system, e.g. Walby’s six structures).
  • Interactionism (micro) focuses on face-to-face interaction, labelling and the subjective meanings individuals construct. Becker’s concept of master status (1963) is the key interactionist contribution to understanding how labels shape behaviour through the self-fulfilling prophecy.

Arguments in favour: functionalism explains social order, the role of socialisation and the positive functions institutions perform; value consensus explains widespread compliance with norms. Arguments against: Marxists argue functionalism ignores class exploitation and that institutions serve ruling-class interests rather than society as a whole; feminists argue functionalism normalises patriarchal family structures (e.g. Parsons' expressive/instrumental roles); interactionists argue it ignores agency, meaning and the effects of labelling. At least two contrasting perspectives and named sociologists are cited. A clear, supported judgement weighing the perspectives. Sustained sociological vocabulary.

Secure: Both support and criticism of functionalism addressed. At least one named alternative perspective cited. A judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly descriptive of functionalism. Some reference to criticism but undeveloped. Conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic description of what functionalism is. Little comparison with other perspectives. No clear judgement.

source.content_html:
Choosing a Research Method

Sociologists have a range of methods available when collecting primary data. The choice of method is never arbitrary — it is shaped by the research question, the population being studied, practical constraints such as time and cost, ethical considerations, and the theoretical perspective of the researcher. An interactionist studying how teachers construct expectations of pupils would choose a very different method from a positivist measuring national rates of educational achievement. This lesson covers the three main families of methods: questionnaires, interviews and observation.

Questionnaires

A questionnaire is a standardised set of written questions distributed to a sample. Closed questions offer a fixed set of responses (e.g. yes/no, tick all that apply, a rating scale from 1 to 5) and produce quantitative data. Open questions allow respondents to answer in their own words, producing qualitative data.

Strengths of questionnaires: They can reach large samples quickly and cheaply, especially via online distribution. They allow statistical analysis and comparison across groups. Responses are anonymous, which may encourage honest answers on sensitive topics. They are standardised — all respondents answer the same questions — which improves reliability (the study could be replicated and compared). Weaknesses: Response rates can be low, introducing bias if non-respondents differ systematically from respondents. Closed questions impose the researcher’s categories on respondents’ experience. Questionnaires cannot probe or follow up unexpected answers, and they assume all respondents interpret questions in the same way — which may not be the case across different social groups.

Key Fact

Questionnaires are high in reliability and allow statistical comparison across large samples, making them the preferred method for positivist sociologists. Their weakness is low validity — closed questions may not capture how respondents really think or feel.

Interviews

A sociological interview involves a researcher asking questions directly of participants. The degree of structure varies significantly:

  • Structured interview: the interviewer follows a fixed schedule of questions in the same order and wording for every participant, much like a spoken questionnaire. This produces quantitative data that is easy to compare across respondents. The weakness is limited depth — no follow-up is possible.
  • Unstructured interview: the interviewer begins with an opening topic and allows the conversation to develop naturally. This resembles an informal conversation and can reveal unexpected themes and rich qualitative data. The weakness is that it is time-consuming, difficult to compare across participants, and the results may reflect the relationship between interviewer and respondent (interviewer effect).
  • Semi-structured interview: uses a list of key themes but allows the interviewer to probe and follow up. It combines some comparability with depth.

A critical evaluative point: interviews can be affected by the interviewer effect — respondents may give socially desirable answers rather than honest ones, particularly on sensitive topics such as domestic violence, drug use or attitudes to ethnicity. They may adjust their answers depending on the perceived social characteristics of the interviewer (age, gender, ethnicity, accent).

A sociologist wants to investigate the experiences of women who have left violent relationships. A structured interview would be inappropriate: the fixed questions might miss the aspects of the experience that matter most to the participants, and the formal tone could feel clinical and discouraging for respondents discussing trauma. An unstructured interview would allow participants to lead the conversation, reveal their own frameworks of meaning, and build the rapport needed to discuss sensitive experiences honestly. The weakness is that the resulting data would be harder to compare systematically across participants. The researcher might use semi-structured interviews as a compromise: key themes guide the conversation but the interviewer follows up where the participant goes.

Observation: Participant and Non-Participant

Observation involves directly watching people in their natural social setting. There are two main variants:

Non-participant observation — the researcher watches without taking part. Strengths: the observer remains detached, reducing the risk of “going native” (over-identifying with the group). Weaknesses: the presence of an observer may alter participants’ behaviour (the Hawthorne effect); the observer cannot access the meanings and motivations behind the behaviour they see.

Participant observation — the researcher joins the group and participates in their daily life, either overtly (with the group’s knowledge) or covertly (without it). Willis’s 1977 study Learning to Labour is a classic example: Willis spent time with twelve working-class boys (whom he called “the lads”) in their school and outside it, observing how they actively resisted school culture and produced their own counter-school subculture. This gave him qualitative depth that no survey could have produced. The strength of participant observation is validity — the data reflects real behaviour in natural settings. The weakness is that it is time-consuming, the researcher may influence the group (reactivity), and covert observation raises serious ethical concerns about deception.

Key Fact

The distinction between reliability (can the study be repeated with the same results?) and validity (does the study measure what it claims to, reflecting real behaviour?) is central to methods evaluation. Questionnaires tend to score well on reliability; participant observation tends to score well on validity. Many methods trade one off against the other.

Mixed Methods and Triangulation

Rather than choosing one method, many sociologists use a mixed methods approach. For example, a study of gender inequality in the workplace might begin with a large-scale questionnaire to identify patterns (quantitative), then follow up with in-depth interviews with selected participants to explore the meanings behind those patterns (qualitative). This strategy is sometimes called triangulation — using multiple methods or data sources so that the weaknesses of one approach are compensated for by the strengths of another.

A critical mistake on methods questions is listing generic strengths and weaknesses without applying them to the specific research context. “Observation is time-consuming” earns limited credit. “Participant observation would be particularly problematic for a study of gang violence because gaining covert access to a criminal network would put the researcher at significant personal risk and would require sustained deception, raising serious ethical concerns about informed consent” earns full credit. The spec explicitly requires students to “identify and explain the advantages and disadvantages, strengths and weaknesses of a particular method for a specific area of research.” Every evaluation point must be anchored to the research topic.
source.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Discuss on research methods, you are almost always asked to evaluate whether a particular method is appropriate for a specific type of research. The best answers structure their argument around three dimensions: practical (is it affordable and accessible?), ethical (does it protect participants?), and theoretical (does the method align with what the researcher wants to know — patterns vs meanings?). A Mastering-tier answer will use all three dimensions and anchor every point to the specific research context stated in the question. Avoid the trap of listing “pros and cons” symmetrically without making a judgement: the question asks “how far” would sociologists agree, so you must weigh the evidence and reach a supported conclusion.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Questionnaires are quick, large-scale and standardised (strengths: reliability, comparability) but may have low response rates and cannot probe answers (weaknesses). Closed questions give quantitative data; open questions give qualitative data.
  • Interviews range from structured (comparable, less depth) to unstructured (more depth, less comparable). All interviews risk the interviewer effect. Willis’s participant observation study Learning to Labour (1977) shows the validity advantage of immersive qualitative research.
  • Reliability (replicability) and validity (truthfulness to real behaviour) are the key evaluative concepts. Mixed methods and triangulation combine methods to exploit their complementary strengths. All evaluation must be applied to the specific research context, not stated as generic lists.

source.content_html:
Why Practical and Ethical Issues Matter

Even the most theoretically sophisticated research design is worthless if it cannot be put into practice or if it causes harm to the people involved. The AQA specification requires students to understand two distinct categories of constraints on sociological research: practical issues (the real-world limitations of time, cost and access) and ethical issues (the moral obligations researchers owe to participants and to society). Crucially, the spec asks not only that students identify these issues but that they explain how researchers address them.

Practical Issues: Time, Cost and Access

Time is a fundamental constraint. A longitudinal study tracking a cohort of children from birth to adulthood might take decades to produce findings — valuable, but beyond the resources of most researchers. A PhD student conducting a dissertation study has months, not years. The method must match the available timescale: participant observation is time-intensive; a self-completion questionnaire distributed via email is not.

Cost constrains the scale and type of research. A large-scale national survey with a team of interviewers and a random sample of 5,000 households requires substantial funding. Academic sociologists apply to research councils; independent researchers may be limited to small local studies. Online questionnaires have dramatically reduced the cost of reaching large samples, but interviewer-led or observational methods remain expensive in labour time.

Access is often the decisive practical constraint. Some groups are hard to reach: gang members, people experiencing domestic abuse, children in care, undocumented migrants. Gatekeepers — head teachers, prison governors, social workers, community leaders — must often be persuaded before the researcher can reach participants at all. Gatekeepers can improve access but can also limit it: a head teacher who restricts research to “well-behaved” pupils introduces sampling bias by excluding the most relevant participants for a study of school exclusion.

Key Fact

The three practical issues are time, cost and access. All three affect which method is feasible and whether the resulting sample will be representative. Access is often the most sociologically interesting: the hardest populations to reach are frequently those whose experiences are most poorly understood and most important to study.

Ethical Issues: Consent, Confidentiality and Harm

The British Sociological Association (BSA) publishes ethical guidelines that professional sociologists are expected to follow. At GCSE level, three ethical issues are named in the specification: informed consent, confidentiality and harm to participants.

Informed consent means participants must be told — in plain language — what the study is about, how their data will be used, and that they can withdraw at any time without penalty. The “informed” element is crucial: obtaining permission for a vaguely described study is not genuine consent. The “voluntary” element is also critical: participants in a prison, a school or a workplace may feel unable to refuse without consequences, even if they are technically told they can.

Confidentiality means that identifying information about participants must be protected. In practice, this means anonymising names and locations in published findings, storing data securely, and not sharing raw data in ways that allow individuals to be identified. Even where participants have consented to take part, they have a right to expect that personal details will not be disclosed to employers, family members or the authorities.

Harm to participants covers a wide range of potential risks: psychological distress from discussing traumatic experiences, physical risk from studying dangerous settings, reputational damage from being identified in publications, or criminal liability from disclosing involvement in illegal activities. The researcher has a duty to anticipate and minimise these risks, not simply to note that they exist.

The spec explicitly asks how ethical issues can be addressed. Students should know practical solutions, not just list the problems:

  • Informed consent: use a written consent form in plain English; for children, obtain parental consent as well; include a clear explanation of withdrawal rights at the start of every session.
  • Confidentiality: anonymise all names and locations in transcripts and publications; use participant codes rather than names in data files; store data on password-protected systems; delete raw recordings after transcription.
  • Harm: offer a debrief session after the research, particularly if sensitive topics were discussed; provide signposting to support services (e.g. domestic abuse helplines); have a clear protocol for stopping the research if a participant shows signs of distress; obtain ethics committee approval before beginning.
  • Deception: covert research necessarily involves deception, which violates the BSA’s informed consent principle. Researchers must justify covert methods by arguing that the social benefit of the knowledge justifies the ethical cost, and must debrief participants as soon as possible after completion.

The Tension Between Research Goals and Ethics

Ethical requirements can directly conflict with research goals. Informed consent can alter participants’ behaviour (if people know they are being studied, they may act differently — the Hawthorne effect). Confidentiality limits what researchers can report. Harm avoidance may prevent researchers from accessing the most important settings. A sociologist wanting to study violence within prison gangs faces an almost irresolvable tension: the most valid data would come from covert observation or candid interviews, but gaining access covertly is deceptive and putting researchers in a violent environment raises serious safety concerns.

Different sociological perspectives can also generate different ethical pressures. A feminist researcher studying violence against women may feel ethically obliged to empower participants rather than simply extract data from them — an approach sometimes called participatory research, in which participants are involved in shaping the research process. A positivist researcher, by contrast, may prioritise objectivity and distance, arguing that participant involvement would compromise validity.

A persistent exam error is to list “consent, confidentiality, harm” as three boxes to tick without reasoning about which apply to the specific research scenario and how the researcher addresses them. For a study of attitudes to unemployment benefit, harm is a relatively minor concern; confidentiality is important but straightforwardly addressed through anonymisation. For a study of underage gang members using covert observation, harm (to participants and researcher), deception (violating informed consent), confidentiality (disclosures of criminal activity) and access (via gatekeepers or snowball sampling) are all live and interconnected problems that require specific, reasoned responses. The mark scheme rewards practical reasoning in context, not a generic list.

Key Fact

Ethical issues in sociological research are not abstract principles but practical problems with practical solutions. Informed consent → written consent form + right to withdraw. Confidentiality → anonymisation + secure data storage. Harm → debrief + support signposting + ethics committee approval. Covert research violates informed consent but may be justified where the study could not be done otherwise and the social value is high.
source.exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark Identify and Describe question on ethical issues, identify a specific issue (not just “ethics”) and describe both what the problem is and how a researcher would address it. The common error is to describe the problem at length without proposing a practical solution. For a 12-mark Discuss on whether ethical constraints make certain research impossible or inadvisable, structure your argument around specific methods and contexts: e.g. covert participant observation of a criminal network is ethically problematic (deception violates informed consent, researcher safety) but may be the only method that produces valid data. A Mastering answer weighs the ethical cost against the research benefit and reaches a clear judgement, rather than simply listing both sides in parallel. Never treat the three ethical principles as a checklist — always apply them to the specific research scenario in the question.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Practical constraints on research are time (affects method choice), cost (limits scale) and access (gatekeepers control entry to populations; hard-to-reach groups require alternative sampling strategies such as snowball sampling).
  • Three ethical principles: informed consent (voluntary agreement after full information), confidentiality (protecting identifying information) and harm to participants (minimising psychological, physical and reputational risk). Each has practical solutions: consent forms, anonymisation, debrief sessions, ethics committee approval.
  • Ethics are not a checklist — they must be applied to the specific research context. Covert observation violates informed consent but may be justified for hard-to-access populations where the social benefit is high. The tension between research goals and ethical obligations is a real and ongoing feature of sociological practice.

Planning Research: Aims, Hypotheses and Pilot Studies

Before collecting a single piece of data, sociologists must make a series of decisions about what they want to find out and how. Research aims define the purpose of a study — for example, “to investigate factors affecting GCSE attainment among students from different socioeconomic backgrounds.” From the aim, the researcher usually develops a hypothesis — a precise, testable prediction, such as “students eligible for free school meals will achieve lower GCSE grades than those who are not.” The hypothesis gives the research direction and allows the findings to be evaluated.

A pilot study is a small-scale test of the research instrument before the main study begins. Imagine a sociologist designing a questionnaire to study attitudes to arranged marriage among young adults in the East Midlands. Running the questionnaire with ten participants first might reveal that a key question is ambiguous, that the response options are too few, or that the time taken is longer than expected. Pilot studies save time and resources by identifying flaws before they contaminate the main data.

Key Fact

The research design process follows a sequence: aim (what do you want to find out?) → hypothesis (what do you predict?) → method choice (how will you gather data?) → sampling (who will you study?) → pilot study (test and refine) → main data collection → analysis.

Sampling: Who to Study?

Sociologists rarely study entire populations. Instead, they select a sample from a sampling frame (a list of the population). The goal is usually a representative sample — one that accurately reflects the characteristics of the wider population, so that findings can be generalised beyond the sample itself.

There are five main sampling methods you need to know:

  • Random sample — every member of the sampling frame has an equal chance of selection. This minimises bias but requires a complete list of the population.
  • Systematic sample — every nth person from the list is selected (e.g. every tenth name). Practical but may introduce bias if the list has a pattern at every nth interval.
  • Stratified sample — the population is divided into groups (strata) by relevant characteristics (e.g. social class, gender) and a proportional number is selected from each stratum. This ensures the sample mirrors the structure of the population.
  • Quota sample — the researcher sets quotas for particular groups (e.g. 50 working-class women, 50 middle-class women) and then selects participants non-randomly until quotas are filled. Quick and inexpensive but non-random, so technically not fully representative.
  • Snowball sample — initial participants recruit others from their networks. Useful for hidden or hard-to-reach populations (e.g. studying drug use, gang membership), but the sample is unlikely to be representative of a wider population.

A sociologist wants to investigate attitudes to higher education among Year 11 students at a comprehensive school in South Yorkshire. The school has 200 Year 11 students. Using a stratified sample, the researcher identifies key strata (e.g. gender, eligibility for free school meals, ethnicity) and selects a proportional number from each group. This increases representativeness — if 30% of students are eligible for free school meals, approximately 30% of the sample will be too, ensuring the findings reflect the full diversity of the year group. A snowball sample would be inappropriate here because students are not a hard-to-reach population and the resulting sample would be biased towards social networks.

Types of Data: Quantitative and Qualitative

Quantitative data takes numerical form — percentages, rates, frequencies, scores. It allows comparisons across large samples, can be analysed statistically, and is associated with approaches that aim for objectivity and replicability. A national survey of 10,000 households can identify patterns and trends in family forms, income or crime rates with a precision no qualitative study can match.

Qualitative data takes verbal form — the words, accounts, feelings and interpretations of research participants. It provides depth and texture, exploring the meanings behind behaviour. An in-depth interview with a family discussing domestic division of labour may reveal nuances about negotiation, resentment and expectation that a tick-box questionnaire would miss entirely.

The choice between quantitative and qualitative approaches often reflects the sociologist’s theoretical perspective. Positivists (associated with functionalism and some Marxist approaches) prefer quantitative data, arguing sociology should emulate natural science. Interpretivists (associated with interactionism) prefer qualitative data, arguing that understanding social behaviour requires grasping the subjective meanings of the participants. In practice, many researchers use mixed methods — combining both types to exploit their complementary strengths.

Primary and Secondary Data; Official Statistics

Primary data is original data collected directly by the researcher. Secondary data is data already gathered by someone else that the researcher re-uses — government statistics, newspaper archives, historical records, published studies.

A very common error is to treat official statistics — figures produced by government departments such as ONS or the Home Office — as straightforward facts. Sociologists are trained to evaluate them critically. Official statistics have strengths: they are large-scale, nationally consistent, free to use, and allow trends to be tracked over time. However, they have important limitations. Crime statistics, for example, only count crimes that are reported to and recorded by the police; the “dark figure” of unreported and unrecorded crime means official figures systematically underestimate the true level of offending. Different perspectives also interpret the same statistics differently: a functionalist might see declining crime rates as evidence of effective social control; a Marxist might argue that statistics reflect selective policing of working-class communities; an interactionist might argue the statistics tell us more about police labelling practices than about actual behaviour. Always evaluate, never just cite.

Key Fact

The five sampling methods are: random, systematic, stratified, quota and snowball. Stratified sampling is best when the researcher wants the sample to mirror the social structure of the population. Snowball sampling is best for hard-to-reach populations where a sampling frame does not exist.
source.exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe about data types or sampling, avoid listing without explaining. A common exam error is to write “quantitative data is numerical and qualitative data is words” and stop there — that is two identifications, not two descriptions. For 4 marks you need to develop each point: explain what makes numerical data useful for sociological research (large-scale, statistically testable, comparable across groups) and what makes qualitative data useful (depth, explores meanings, reveals what statistics miss). Linking to a named method or theoretical perspective (e.g. “positivists prefer quantitative data because…”) lifts the answer further. On the 12-mark Discuss, evaluation of official statistics must be in context — not just “statistics can be wrong” but explaining exactly why the specific statistics are problematic for the research question.
source.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Research design follows a sequence: aim → hypothesis → method → sampling → pilot study → data collection → analysis. Pilot studies test and refine instruments before the main study.
  • Five sampling methods: random (equal chance), systematic (every nth), stratified (proportional by group), quota (non-random quotas) and snowball (for hard-to-reach populations). The aim is a representative sample that allows findings to be generalised.
  • Quantitative data (numbers) suits large-scale pattern-finding; qualitative data (words) suits in-depth meaning. Official statistics are secondary data with both strengths (scale, consistency) and weaknesses (under-reporting, political production) that sociologists must always evaluate critically.

practice_questions.text:
Which sampling method involves selecting every tenth person from a list of the population?
A) Random sample
B) Quota sample
C) Systematic sample
D) Snowball sample
practice_questions.marks: C) Systematic sample [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'hypothesis' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating a hypothesis is a prediction or statement to be tested; 1 mark for indicating it predicts a relationship between variables and can be supported or refuted by evidence. Example: 'A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction about a relationship between two or more variables, stated before data collection and either supported or refuted by the findings.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one advantage of using a pilot study and describe how it would improve the quality of a sociological investigation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage (e.g. identifies flaws in questions, reveals ambiguity, indicates how long the study will take, tests whether the sampling method is practical). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying that a pilot study identifies ambiguous questions (1 mark) and explaining that if a question is unclear to respondents, different participants will interpret it differently, reducing the validity and reliability of the data; revising the question after the pilot ensures all participants understand it in the same way (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between quantitative and qualitative data, and explain why sociologists might choose one over the other.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for describing the difference: quantitative data is numerical (percentages, rates, counts) and allows statistical analysis and large-scale comparison; qualitative data is verbal (words, accounts, meanings) and provides depth and insight into participants' experiences. Up to 2 marks for explaining a reason to choose one. Example: a sociologist studying national patterns of divorce might choose quantitative data (ONS statistics) because it allows trends over time to be identified across the whole population; a sociologist studying the experience of family breakdown for individual children might choose qualitative data (in-depth interviews) because the lived experience requires depth of understanding that statistics cannot provide.

practice_questions.text: Identify one limitation of using official statistics as a source of data in sociological research and describe how this affects the validity of conclusions drawn from them.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a limitation of official statistics (e.g. under-reporting, dark figure of crime, political production, recording inconsistencies between police forces, changing legal definitions). Up to 2 marks for developing the description. Example: identifying under-reporting (1 mark) and explaining that many crimes are never reported to the police — particularly domestic violence and sexual assault — so official crime statistics significantly undercount the true level of offending; any conclusions about crime patterns drawn from official statistics may therefore reflect reporting behaviour rather than actual crime, threatening the validity of the findings (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: "Official statistics are the most useful source of data for sociological research." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour include: official statistics cover the entire population, are free to access, allow long-term trend analysis, and carry the authority of consistent national collection (e.g. ONS, Crime Survey for England and Wales). Arguments against include: official statistics are produced by governments and may reflect political priorities; crime statistics are limited by the dark figure of unreported and unrecorded crime; different sociological perspectives interpret the same statistics differently (functionalist, Marxist and interactionist readings of crime data diverge significantly); qualitative data may offer insight that statistics obscure. The answer cites at least two sociological perspectives or contexts (e.g. crime vs family research), evaluates specific strengths and weaknesses in context, and reaches a clear supported judgement. Sustained sociological vocabulary.

Secure: Both strengths and limitations addressed. At least one sociological perspective cited. A judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive. Some evaluation but undeveloped. Conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic points about what statistics are. Little evaluation. No clear judgement.
